title: Event-driven batch ingest connector: enterprise integration guide
author: Maya Patel
body:
Summary
This guide describes a recommended, production-ready approach for integrating event-driven batch ingestion pipelines with the Redwood Inference platform. It targets enterprise customers that ingest large volumes of user events (logs, suggestions, or telemetry) in batches and call Redwood models for enrichment, reranking, or embeddings. The pattern covers connector architecture, configuration, resiliency, monitoring, and an escalation matrix for operational issues.

Audience
- Customer Success Engineers (CSEs) onboarding enterprise customers
- Platform/ML Engineers building connectors to Redwood APIs
- SREs owning the ingestion pipeline and monitoring

Goals
1. Provide a deterministic, cost-effective pattern for batched inference with event-driven triggers.
2. Minimize per-token cost via caching and batching policies while preserving SLOs.
3. Document operational runbook for common failure modes and escalation.

Scope and non-goals
- This document focuses on event-to-batch pipelines that call Redwood’s REST API or Private Connector. It does NOT cover one-off interactive chat integrations or client-side SDK usage.

High-level architecture
1) Event producer: customer service emits events into a durable queue (Kafka topic, Kinesis stream, or SQS).
2) Batcher/connector: our recommended connector groups events by tenant/model and prepares batched requests using prefix/KV cache hints.
3) Redwood frontdoor: requests are sent to Redwood Routed API endpoint or Private connector (VPC) based on customer deployment.
4) Post-processing: enrichment service applies business logic, writes results to datastore (BigQuery/Snowflake/S3) and triggers downstream workflows.

Text diagram (logical)
Event producer -> Kafka (topic: events-ingest) -> Connector (batcher) -> Redwood API/Private -> Enricher -> Storage

Prerequisites and requirements
- Accounts: Customer must have a Redwood API key with batch ingestion scope and (for Private) VPN peering configured.
- Networking: outbound egress to Redwood endpoints or VPC peering for Private deployments. TLS 1.2+.
- Quotas: agreed throughput (tokens/sec) per tenant. Confirm Dedicated capacity commitments if > 10k concurrent tokens/sec.
- Security: KMS integration for any customer-managed keys when using Private.

Configuration checklist (table-style text)
- Connector concurrency: default 8 workers per vCPU (adjust after testing).
- Batch window: 250 ms or 1,000 events, whichever comes first.
- Max tokens per batch: 65,536 tokens (model-specific — align with model's sequence length).
- Retry policy: exponential backoff starting at 200ms, max 60s, 5 attempts.
- Circuit breaker: open after 50% error rate over 1-minute sliding window; rampdown to 10% traffic on fallback model.

Sample connector configuration (YAML)
```
connector:
  type: kafka-consumer
  topics:
    - events-ingest
  batch:
    max_events: 1000
    max_wait_ms: 250
    max_tokens: 65536
  concurrency: 8
  retry:
    max_attempts: 5
    base_backoff_ms: 200
    max_backoff_ms: 60000
  circuit_breaker:
    error_threshold_pct: 50
    window_sec: 60
    fallback_ratio: 0.1
  redwood_endpoint: "https://api.redwood-inference.com/v1/batch"
  api_key_source: "vault:kms/redwood-service-account"
```

Batch formation guidelines
- Group by tenant and model variant to maximize cache hits (same model+prompt structure yields KV cache reuse).
- Preserve ordering for time-series dependent events; otherwise process out-of-order to increase batching.
- Attach deterministic prompt templates to avoid quality variance across batches.

Call pattern and payload example
- Use Redwood batch endpoint with array-of-requests payload. Each item should include: tenant_id, request_id, prompt, hints (cache_prefix), and metadata.
- Example payload snippet:
```
POST /v1/batch
Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED_API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "requests": [
    {"tenant_id":"acct-123","request_id":"r-1","prompt":"Summarize: ...","cache_hint":"acct-123:summary-v1"},
    {"tenant_id":"acct-123","request_id":"r-2","prompt":"Summarize: ...","cache_hint":"acct-123:summary-v1"}
  ],
  "model": "redwood-rlhf-7b-v2",
  "max_tokens": 256
}
```

Monitoring and SLOs
- Recommended SLOs for batch ingestion:
  - Availability: 99.95% (API success responses within SLA window).
  - P99 end-to-end processing latency (producer -> storage): <= 2s for small batches, <= 10s for large batches.
  - Error budget: 0.05% monthly.
- Essential metrics to ship to dashboards:
  - redwood.requests.total, redwood.requests.success, redwood.requests.errors (4xx/5xx split), redwood.tokens.consumed, connector.batch.size, connector.latency_ms, connector.retries.count, connector.circuit_breaker_state
- Alerts (examples):
  1) P95 batch latency > 5s for 5m -> page on-call SRE.
  2) Error rate > 5% for same model for 3m -> open incident and escalate to Redwood CSE.
  3) Token consumption spike > 3x forecast -> notify Finance + Sales.

Logging and tracing
- Include request_id and batch_id in all logs.
- Trace Redwood API calls using X-Trace-Id: <guid> and link traces in Redwood Console -> trace view.
- Persist sample error payloads (redacted PII) for triage.

Cost optimizations and guardrails
- Use prefix/KV caching hints to reuse compute when prompts share prefixes.
- Prefer streaming where forwarded responses are large and single-threaded.
- Enforce per-tenant daily token caps via rate-limiter to avoid runaway costs.

Failure modes and workarounds
1) 5xx spikes from Redwood API
   - Short-term: activate circuit breaker and switch 10% traffic to a lower-cost fallback model (e.g., redwood-rlhf-3b-quant) configured in connector.
   - Long-term: collect request_ids and open a support ticket via Redwood Console with timeline, sample payloads, and relevant trace ids.
2) Partial batch failures (some items succeed)
   - Best practice: connector must implement item-level retries. Mark successful items as complete; enqueue failed items to retry queue with exponential backoff.
3) Network flaps / DNS issues
   - Workaround: implement client-side DNS caching and fallback to Private connector or alternate region endpoint.
4) Cost surge due to malformed prompts
   - Apply server-side schema validation to reject unexpectedly large prompts; alert product owner and block offending keys until fixed.

Testing and validation checklist
- Unit tests for batcher logic and token counting.
- Integration test: synthetic load test at 2x expected peak for 30 minutes. Verify token consumption, latency SLOs, and error behavior.
- Canary rollout: start at 1% traffic for 30 minutes, 5% for 2 hours, 25% for 24 hours, then 100%.
- Regression tests: prompt set-based QA to compare output distributions between model variants.

Operational runbook (step-by-step)
1) Detection: alert triggers or user report indicating high errors or latency.
2) Triage (5 minutes): check connector logs, batch failure rate, Redwood Console for downstream errors, token usage spike.
3) Immediate mitigation (10 minutes): reduce connector concurrency by 50%, enable fallback model at 10% traffic, increase batch window to 500ms to reduce API QPS.
4) Escalation (30 minutes): if errors persist, open Redwood support case (include request_ids, traces, sample payloads) and notify CSE and Account Exec.
5) Post-incident (72 hours): run RCA with customer and Redwood team, document mitigations and follow-up actions.

Escalation contacts and SLAs
- On-call SRE (customer): Pager duty team (customer side) — primary contact.
- Redwood CSE: cse-oncall@redwood.ai (weekday 08:00–18:00 PT) — response target 1 hour.
- Redwood SRE escalation: sre-escalations@redwood.ai — response target 30 minutes for P1.
- For Private deployments include VPN and account team contacts (see customer onboarding packet).

Known limitations and recommended workarounds
- Model sequence-length limits: extremely long concatenated contexts may require chunking; prefer semantic chunking and reassembly.
- KV cache misses on heterogeneous prompts: group by prompt template to improve hit rate.
- Batch size vs. latency tradeoff: large batches improve cost but increase tail-latency — use dynamic batch tuning tied to latency budgets.

Appendix A: Sample end-to-end curl test
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood-inference.com/v1/batch \ 
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${REDWOOD_API_KEY}" \ 
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ 
  -d '{"model":"redwood-rlhf-7b-v2","requests":[{"tenant_id":"acct-123","request_id":"t-1","prompt":"Short summary of text A","cache_hint":"acct-123:summ-v1"}] }'
```

Appendix B: Onboarding checklist for CSE
- Verify API keys + scopes and networking (egress or VPC).
- Confirm Dedicated capacity or Private SLA if required.
- Deploy connector in staging and run integration test harness.
- Review dashboards with customer: token burn, latency, failure rates.
- Schedule QBR in 30 days to review quality metrics and cost.

Ownership and follow-ups
- Connector template maintenance: Platform Eng.
- Customer onboarding operational owner: assigned CSE (see related page for handoff).
- Billing anomalies: Finance + Account Exec.

End of document
